1:
TEACHER NOTES:
This title slide opens Lesson 6. Have pencil, mini whiteboards, textas and booklets out before you click off this slide.
2:
TEACHER NOTES:
Planning slide for the teacher. The Extended Path is the 60 minute version, so use the full deck unless your time slot is shorter. No student talk needed here.
3:
TEACHER NOTES:
Pre-read the matching Teacher Handbook and pages 1 to 29 of A Year on our Farm before teaching. Decide your pause points and any incidental vocabulary in advance, since they are not pre-set on the slides.
4:
TEACHER NOTES:
Quick icon reference. I = I do (modelling), W = We do (guided), CfU = Check for understanding, Y = You do (independent practice). Skip past for students.
5:
TEACHER NOTES:
Legend for student response routines used through the deck. Whiteboard response, choral response, thumbs and show fingers come up most often. Boards and textas should already be out from slide 8.
6:
TEACHER NOTES:
Icon legend only. No teaching action required.
7:
TEACHER NOTES:
Reference chart for the colour coded sentence parts. Use only if you plan to colour code parts of speech today; otherwise skip.
8:
SAY:
- "We need three things on our desks."
- "Pencil. Mini whiteboard with a texta. Booklet."
- "Show me your texta up high when you are ready."

DO:
- Point to each item on the slide as students get it out.
- Wait until every student has all three before moving on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick set up slide. Do not start the read aloud until every student has a board and a working texta.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with no texta or a dry texta. Top up before reading begins.
9:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for the shared reading. Use it to settle the class. Hold the book up and remind students that listening eyes are on the cover.
10:
SAY:
- "Eyes on the cover. What do you notice?"
- "Read with me as I turn each page."
- "Ask: how do the pictures help us understand the story? Expected: the pictures show what the family is doing and what the farm looks like."
- "Point to one picture that helped you understand the words."

DO:
- Hold the book so the whole class can see each illustration.
- Pause at the points you chose from the Teacher Handbook and ask one quick comprehension question at each pause.
- Take 2 to 3 student responses about how the pictures help.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the shared read aloud of pages 1 to 29. Pause points and incidental vocabulary are not supplied on the slide, so plan them in advance from the Teacher Handbook. Keep the focus on how illustrations support meaning, not on every detail of the text.

WATCH FOR:
- Students naming colours only. Prompt: "What is happening in the picture? How does that help us know what is going on?"
- Students who lose focus during a long page. Pause and ask one student to point to the next picture.
11:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the writing focus on nouns. Reset the room: book away, boards out, eyes up. Move to slide 12 once everyone is ready.
12:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "A noun is a word that names a person, place, animal or thing."
- "There are two kinds. Common nouns are general names. Proper nouns name a specific one and start with a capital letter."
- "Point to ball. Ball names a thing. So ball is a noun. It is not one special ball, so it is a common noun. No capital."
- "Point to David. David names one special person. So David is a proper noun. Capital D."

DO:
- Point to each picture and word as you say it.
- Tap the capital D on David and the capital A on Australia.
- Keep boards down. Students watch and listen on this slide.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is explicit modelling. The two ideas to land are "names" (it is a noun) and "specific one" (it needs a capital). Keep it short.

MISCONCEPTIONS:
- Misconception: any important word needs a capital letter.
  Why: students see capitals on signs, titles and at the start of sentences.
  Impact: students over-capitalise common nouns like ball or chicken.
  Quick correction: ask "Is this one special ball, or any ball?" If any, no capital.

WATCH FOR:
- Students mouthing the words but not watching the screen. Bring eyes back before you continue.
13:
SAY:
- "Read with me: The dog sleeps in the shed."
- "I am looking for words that name an animal, a place, a person or a thing."
- "Dog names an animal. Shed names a place. Both are nouns."
- "Are they special names? No. Any dog. Any shed. So they are common nouns. No capital letter."

DO:
- Read the sentence aloud, pointing to each word.
- Circle dog and shed on the screen with your finger or pointer.
- Keep boards down. Students watch.

TEACHER NOTES:
First worked example. The teacher does the thinking out loud. Students should not write yet.

WATCH FOR:
- Students calling out other words. Acknowledge briefly, then bring them back to dog and shed.
14:
SAY:
- "Read with me: Maria the cat sleeps in the shed."
- "Maria is a name for one special cat."
- "Because Maria is a special name, it starts with a capital M. So Maria is a proper noun."
- "Cat and shed are still common nouns. They are general words."

DO:
- Point to the capital M on Maria.
- Compare with slide 13 by gesture: "Last sentence had no name. This one has Maria."
- Keep your voice on the word "special" each time.

TEACHER NOTES:
Builds directly on slide 13. The change is that one cat now has a name, and the capital letter is the visible signal.

WATCH FOR:
- Students wanting to capitalise cat as well. Remind them cat is the type, not the name.
15:
SAY:
- "Read with me: The children help dad feed the sheep."
- "On your board, write the nouns you can find."
- "Show me."
- "Ask: does dad need a capital here? Expected: yes, when dad is being used as the name."

DO:
- Give 30 seconds of silent thinking before boards up.
- Reveal the corrected sentence only after you scan every board.
- Point to the capital D when Dad is revealed.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Boards
Script:
- Ask: which words are nouns? Expected: children, dad, sheep.
- Scan for: students writing all three nouns and capitalising Dad.
PROCEED:
- >=80% find the nouns and capitalise Dad. Move to the Mum special case on slide 16.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students leave dad in lowercase.
- Reteach: cover the sentence and ask "Is dad a name here, or a type of person?" Use the visible explanation card on the slide.
- Re-check: try "Her dad was at the park." Ask if dad needs a capital here. Expected: no, because here dad is a type, not a name.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the first special case. Some words like dad are common nouns when used as a type and proper nouns when used as a name.

WATCH FOR:
- Students capitalising feed or sheep too. Quick reminder: only the special name takes the capital.
16:
SAY:
- "Same idea with mum."
- "Read with me: We saw mum in the paddock. Then: We saw Mum in the paddock."
- "Both can be right. It depends on whether mum is being used as a name or as a type."
- "Look at the next two sentences. Show me on your fingers: 1 for proper noun, 2 for common noun."

DO:
- Point to the lowercase mum in "My mum plants trees." Ask: name or type?
- Reveal common noun together.
- Repeat for "Your mum is at the shop."

TEACHER NOTES:
The slide gives two sample sentences to classify. Do not race through. The thinking step is "name or type?" each time.

WATCH FOR:
- Students answering by guess. Ask one student to point to the clue word that helped them decide.
17:
SAY:
- "Each word goes in one of two columns. Common noun or proper noun."
- "Look at horse. Is it a name or a general word?"
- "Show me on your board. Write C for common or P for proper."

DO:
- Read each word aloud once.
- Reveal each match only after boards are up.
- Point to the capital letter on each proper noun as it lands.

TEACHER NOTES:
horse, fence and dam are common. Georgie, November and Kelly are proper. The visible clue is the capital letter on each proper noun.

WATCH FOR:
- Students putting november in the common column because it is lowercase. Quick reminder: months are always proper nouns and need a capital.
18:
SAY:
- "Same routine. Sort each word."
- "Show me C for common or P for proper."
- "Watch for tricky ones like school and wednesday."

DO:
- Read each word aloud once.
- Reveal each correct column after a board scan.
- Tap the capital letter when it lands on Mr Smith, Australia and Wednesday.

TEACHER NOTES:
computer, theatre and school are common. Mr Smith, Australia and Wednesday are proper. Days and months are always proper.

WATCH FOR:
- Students leaving wednesday in the common column. Ask: "Is Wednesday one special day, or any day?" One special day, so capital W.
19:
SAY:
- "Read with me: The cats play with mum."
- "On your board, underline the nouns and add capital letters where they are needed."
- "Remember: mum can be a proper noun when it is used as a name."

DO:
- Give 45 seconds.
- Walk past two or three boards to spot common errors before revealing.
- Reveal Mum with a capital. Underline cats and Mum.

TEACHER NOTES:
Two short sentences. Proper nouns: Mum, Jess. Common nouns: cats, sister, apricots. Use the slide as guided practice, not a test.

WATCH FOR:
- Students capitalising sister. Quick correction: sister is a type, not a name.
20:
SAY:
- "Read with me: The cheeky cat plays with mum in the garden."
- "Underline only the nouns. Words like cheeky and juicy describe the noun, but they are not nouns."
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Point to cheeky and juicy to show they are not nouns.
- Reveal cat, Mum and garden as the nouns. For the second sentence reveal sister, Jess, apricots and orchard.

TEACHER NOTES:
This adds adjectives to push students to focus on naming words only. Keep it brief.

WATCH FOR:
- Students underlining cheeky or juicy. Quick correction: "Does cheeky name something? No, it tells us about the cat."
21:
SAY:
- "Proper nouns name a specific person, place or thing. Days and months too."
- "Read with me: georgie was chased by the gander on monday."
- "On your board, rewrite this sentence with capital letters where they are needed."
- "Don't forget the full stop at the end."

DO:
- Read the sentence aloud first.
- Wait while students write on boards.
- Reveal Georgie and Monday with capitals, plus the full stop.

TEACHER NOTES:
Two proper nouns to fix (Georgie, Monday) plus the start of sentence capital and end punctuation. Keep the focus on the three things to check.

WATCH FOR:
- Students fixing the names but forgetting the capital G at the start. Quick reminder: every sentence starts with a capital letter.
22:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers which sentence is the right one."
- "Look at every word. Look at the start, the proper nouns and the end."

DO:
- Give think time. Boards down.
- Show fingers up.
- Reveal the correct sentence: Maria tried to catch the parrot.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which sentence is correctly punctuated? Expected: Maria tried to catch the parrot.
- Scan for: most students showing the matching number.
PROCEED:
- >=80% choose the correct option. Move on.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick the option with capital P on Parrot.
- Reteach: ask "Is parrot one special parrot, or any parrot?" Any parrot, so no capital.
- Re-check: try "the dog ran fast." Ask if dog needs a capital here.

TEACHER NOTES:
Three checks: capital M on Maria, no capital on parrot, full stop at the end.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing fast without looking at every part of the sentence. Slow them down.
23:
SAY:
- "Read with me: in march, maria had kittens."
- "Find the proper nouns. Add capital letters. Add a full stop at the end."
- "Show me your board."

DO:
- Read the sentence at a slow pace so all students follow.
- Reveal the corrected sentence only after boards are up.
- Repeat with: lillypilly likes to munch the grass in july.

TEACHER NOTES:
Proper nouns: March, Maria, Lillypilly, July. Plus the capital at the start and the full stop at the end.

WATCH FOR:
- Students missing the capital at the very start of the sentence. Use the editing list on the slide as a checking tool.
24:
SAY:
- "Same job. Find the proper nouns. Add capital letters. Add a full stop."
- "These sentences have extra describing words like friendly, long and green. Do not capitalise those."

DO:
- Read both sentences aloud first.
- Pause for 60 seconds while students write.
- Reveal corrected sentences side by side.

TEACHER NOTES:
Names and months are still the proper nouns. The describing words are decoys to test focus.

WATCH FOR:
- Students capitalising friendly or long. Quick correction: "Does friendly name something? No, it describes."
25:
SAY:
- "Pick a common noun from the first list and write a sentence about it."
- "Pick a proper noun from the second list and write a sentence about it."
- "Capital at the start. Capitals for proper nouns. Full stop at the end."

DO:
- Read both word lists aloud once.
- Show students the two example sentences as models.
- Circulate to support students who need a sentence starter.

TEACHER NOTES:
Short writing on whiteboards. Each student should produce two sentences. Use the slide examples as scaffolds for students who struggle to start.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Use the frame "The ___ was ___." with a chosen common noun.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Write one sentence that uses one common noun and one proper noun together.

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing a noun only, not a sentence. Remind them a sentence needs a doing word too.
26:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Look at the start of the sentence. Look at the proper nouns. Look at the end."

DO:
- Give 20 seconds of silent think time.
- Cue fingers up at the same time.
- Reveal the correct sentences after every student has shown.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which sentence is correctly punctuated? Expected: We find mushrooms in May. Daisy goes in a box filled with hay.
- Scan for: most students showing the matching number for both sets.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to slide 27.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students miss the lowercase "we" at the start, or capitalise Mushrooms.
- Reteach: read both options together and underline the difference.
- Re-check: try a fresh pair like "the cat ate." or "The cat ate."

TEACHER NOTES:
First hinge check before independent work. The two likely mistakes are over-capitalising mushrooms or leaving "we" lowercase.

WATCH FOR:
- Students changing answers when they look at neighbours. Use boards down, think, then show.
27:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Two more sentences. Pick the one that is correct."

DO:
- Same routine: silent think, fingers up, reveal.
- Point to the lowercase carrots and cabbages on the wrong option.

TEACHER NOTES:
The wrong options over-capitalise common nouns (Carrots, Cabbages, Socks, Smoky). The correct sentences capitalise only names and the start of the sentence.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the over-capitalised version. Quick correction: "Are carrots one special vegetable? No, any carrot, so no capital."
28:
SAY:
- "Open your booklet to Lesson 6: Sentence-level writing."
- "Eyes back here when your booklet is open and your pencil is out."

DO:
- Wait until every student has the right page.
- Read the page heading aloud once.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick transition slide to the booklet. Use this moment to reset behaviour before independent work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still on the wrong page. Pause and reset before starting the next slide.
29:
SAY:
- "First task. Sort each word into common noun or proper noun."
- "Work on your own. No talking."

DO:
- Stand near students who often need the first prompt.
- Spot check three students within the first minute.
- Reveal correct columns at the end if you use the slide for whole class checking.

TEACHER NOTES:
cow, farm, tractor, barn are common. Jess, Sunday, January, April are proper. Months and days are always proper.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Cover half the words and sort just the easy ones first (cow, Jess, January).
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Add one more common noun and one more proper noun of their own choice to each column.

WATCH FOR:
- Students leaving january in the common column. Quick reminder: months are always proper nouns.
30:
SAY:
- "Read the passage to yourself first."
- "Then make a list of every proper noun you can find."
- "Use a capital letter at the start of each one."

DO:
- Give 4 to 5 minutes.
- Circulate and check capitalisation on the lists.
- Compare with the highlighted passage when most students have finished.

TEACHER NOTES:
Proper nouns to find: January, Mum, Dad, Jess, Georgie, Maria, March, Tiger. Common nouns are not the focus here.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Underline the capitalised words in the passage first, then copy them into the list.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Sort the list into two groups: people and other (months and animals).

WATCH FOR:
- Students missing Tiger or March. Prompt: "Look again at the second paragraph."
31:
TEACHER NOTES:
Acknowledgement and credits slide. No teaching action required.
